transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what’s been bothering you or what brings you in today?

Well, I suppose I’m here because... it's the datasets. I’m pretty sure the people on that environmental modeling contract have been tracking my revisions. They’re planting errors in the numbers to make it look like I can’t lead the work anymore. My wife keeps saying—and the junior analysts too, they always tell me it's just version-control mistakes. 

Version control. I started working with data back in the 80s, you know. We didn't have these fancy cloud repositories. I had this one professor in college, Dr. Aris, who still kept punch cards in his office just to show us how good we had it. He had this enormous beard, always smelled like pipe tobacco. Cherry wood, I think it was. You really don't see people smoking pipes anymore, do you? It's a shame, it's a very nostalgic smell. Reminds me of autumn. 

But... right, anyway, they are definitely putting errors in my models on purpose to push me out, no matter what my wife says about the software.
Do you believe that these people are intentionally targeting you or trying to harm you in any other way beyond just the errors in the models?

Harm me? I mean... I don't think they're going to jump out of the bushes with a baseball bat or anything. Like I was telling you, it's about the datasets. They are absolutely tracking my revisions on this environmental modeling contract. They wait until I log off, and then they plant errors in the code to make it look like I've lost my touch, like I can't lead the work anymore. And my wife—bless her, she doesn't know anything about data—she and the junior analysts just keep repeating that it’s just version-control mistakes. 

Version control... Everything is about syncing and versions now. My phone is always asking me to update to a new version. It tries to sync with my car. I used to drive this 1998 Honda Civic, didn't need to sync with a single thing. You just put the key in the ignition and drove. It had a tape deck. I used to listen to Fleetwood Mac on cassette on my way to campus. *Rumours*, mostly. Incredible album, really. Though I always felt bad for the band, all that interpersonal drama they had going on behind the scenes. Have you ever seen them live? I went to a show in '82, rained the entire time, my shoes were completely ruined. Mud everywhere. 

But... what was I saying? Right, the contract. No, they aren't trying to hurt me physically. They just want me off the project.
Have you noticed any other unusual experiences, like hearing voices, seeing things that others don't, or feeling like there are hidden messages in everyday events?

Voices? Hidden messages? No, nothing like that. I mean, my hearing isn't what it used to be, but I don't hear anything that isn't there. And I don't see things either, except maybe my glasses being smudged half the time. I've been wearing glasses since I was a teenager. Used to have those thick, awful plastic frames, the ones that covered half your face. You know the kind? They were terrible. I broke a pair playing intramural volleyball once. Took a spike right to the face. The nurse had to pull a little piece of plastic out of my eyebrow. I still have a tiny scar right here. 

Volleyball was big back then. We used to set up a net in the quad on weekends. We had this one guy, Dave, he was about six-foot-four, played like he was trying out for the Olympics. Took it way too seriously. We were just out there having a couple of beers and getting some sun. I wonder whatever happened to Dave. He was a math major too, actually. Always talking about topology. 

But no... no voices or hidden messages or anything like that. Just the numbers in the datasets. That's what's real, and that's where they're messing with me.
Do you believe that the people modifying your datasets are acting as part of a coordinated effort or under direction from someone else?

Coordinated? Well, yes, it has to be. You don't just mess up datasets that massive by yourself. The people on that environmental modeling contract are definitely working together. They track my revisions and then intentionally plant those errors so it looks like I'm losing my edge, like I can't lead the work anymore. No matter how many times my wife or those junior analysts try to tell me it’s just version-control mistakes, I know they're coordinating it behind my back. 

Coordination... you know, it's funny how people coordinate things now. They use all these chat programs. Slack, Teams, whatever it is. Back when I started, if you wanted to coordinate a project, you actually had to sit in a room together. We had this massive conference table at my first job. Solid oak. Must have weighed half a ton. It took four guys just to move it when they decided to recarpet the office. 

They put in this awful, bright orange shag carpet. I guess it was the style back then, but it just gave everyone a headache. If you dropped a paperclip or a pencil eraser in that carpet, it was gone forever. You'd just hear the vacuum cleaner rattling at night when the janitor came through. Frank, his name was. Nice guy, but he complained about that carpet every single night. He had a bad knee, wore one of those heavy metal braces under his trousers. Said it acted up whenever it rained. I always wondered if those old injuries really can predict the weather. My grandfather used to say his shoulder would ache before a thunderstorm, but I never knew if he was just pulling my leg. He was quite the joker, my grandfather. Used to do this trick with a quarter behind my ear...
Do you feel like people are also working against you or plotting against you outside of your work on the environmental modeling contract?

Outside of work? No, no, I don't think so. It's really just the people on that environmental modeling contract. Like I said, I'm here because I'm pretty sure they're tracking my revisions and planting those errors in the datasets to make it look like I can't lead the work. My wife and the junior analysts keep trying to tell me it's just version-control mistakes, but I know what's happening. It's just the work.

Work... you know, I used to work as a busboy when I was in high school. Down at this little diner on Main Street. The Silver Spoon, it was called. Best cherry pie you've ever had. The baker, Mrs. Higgins, she made the crust from scratch every morning. She used lard, which I know nobody does anymore because of cholesterol, but it made all the difference. She had these enormous hands, like a baseball catcher. Always covered in flour. She passed away a few years ago, I think. Or maybe she moved to Florida? A lot of people move to Florida when they get older. The humidity is supposed to be good for your joints, but I can't stand the heat. I went to Orlando once in August, and I felt like I was walking through hot soup. 

But anyway, no, nobody is plotting against me at the grocery store or anything like that. It's just the people on the contract.
Have you ever had any beliefs that others were plotting against you or acting in a coordinated way in other parts of your life, outside of this situation at work?

No, no, I just said that. It's only the people on the environmental modeling contract. Outside of work, everything is fine. Nobody else is doing anything like that. I don't know why you'd think that. It's just the contract. 

Contracts... you know, I bought a car once, and the contract was about fifty pages long. Just for a sedan! It was a Honda Accord, a '98. Great car, actually. Got fantastic gas mileage. I used to drive it up to the mountains on weekends. The air up there is so crisp, you know? Nothing like the city. We used to rent this little cabin near a lake. The water was freezing, even in July, but my kids would jump right in anyway. Kids don't feel the cold, I swear. They'd come out with their lips turning blue, shivering, and ten minutes later they're back in the water. 

I tried to teach my son how to fish up there, but he didn't have the patience for it. You really have to sit still for a long time to catch anything. You just watch the bobber float on the water. It's very peaceful. Unless the mosquitoes are out. One year, the mosquitoes were so bad we had to stay inside the whole weekend playing Monopoly. I hate Monopoly. It never ends. Someone always gets mad and flips the board. Usually my brother, actually. He was a terrible loser. Still is, probably. 

But anyway... no, nobody else is plotting anything. Just the people messing with my datasets at work.
Do you have any objective evidence that your coworkers are intentionally changing your datasets, or is it something you just know based on your experience?

Objective evidence? Well... I mean, I know it based on my experience, yes. I've been doing this a long time. But the evidence is right there in the files. I'm here because I'm pretty sure the people on that environmental modeling contract have been tracking my revisions and planting errors in the datasets to make it look like I can't lead the work. It's obvious to me. Even when my wife or the junior analysts tell me it's just version-control mistakes, I know better. You don't get those kinds of specific errors by accident. 

Accidents... you know, I had an accident once on a bicycle when I was twelve. Went right over the handlebars. Scraped up my knees so bad I couldn't wear long pants for a month. It was summer, anyway, so it didn't matter much, but we were supposed to go to my cousin's wedding. They made me wear these awful scratchy wool trousers. Wool in July! Can you imagine? My aunt insisted on a formal wedding. She was always very proper, my aunt. She had this dining room table that you weren't even allowed to set a glass on without a coaster. God forbid you left a water ring. She had this little dog, too, a Pomeranian, I think. Yappy little thing. It used to sit under the table and bite at your ankles if you moved your feet too much. 

I never understood why people get small dogs. They're basically just loud cats. If you're going to get a dog, you should get a real dog, like a Golden Retriever. We had a Retriever mix when the kids were young. Buster, his name was. He used to chase his own tail until he got dizzy and fell over. It was the funniest thing. But anyway... yes, the evidence is in the datasets. They're definitely doing it on purpose.

Even though your wife and the junior analysts have told you that the errors in the datasets are likely due to version-control issues, do you still feel absolutely certain—without any doubt—that the errors are being planted intentionally by others on the contract?

Yes, absolutely certain. I mean, without a shadow of a doubt. I know my wife and those junior analysts keep parroting the same thing about version-control mistakes, but they just don't see what I see. I'm telling you, I know for a fact that the people on that contract are tracking every single revision I make. They're planting those errors in the datasets specifically to make it look like I'm incompetent and can't lead the work. 

My wife, bless her, she always just looks for the simplest explanation for everything. Like... well, like this one time our old lawnmower wouldn't start. She swore up and down it was just out of gas, but I knew the spark plug was fouled. I used to tinker with small engines a lot back in the eighties. Lawnmowers, weed whackers, leaf blowers, you name it. I had this great little workbench set up in the garage. The whole place always smelled like motor oil and sawdust. I actually built a birdhouse out there once, out of cedar. Cedar has such a distinct smell, doesn't it? It's supposed to keep moths away, too. My grandmother had this huge cedar chest at the foot of her bed where she kept all these heavy winter quilts. She stitched them all by hand, every little square. Must have taken her months to do just one. People don't really make things by hand anymore, do they? Everything is just mass-produced in factories now. It's a real shame, you lose that personal touch. 

But anyway... yeah, I have zero doubt about the datasets. It's not a software glitch, they're doing it to me on purpose.
Do you believe the people planting errors in your datasets have special abilities or powers, or is it something that you think could happen through normal, real-world means like hacking or collusion?

No, no special powers. I mean, they aren't magicians or anything. It's just normal... well, normal for them, I guess. Collusion, hacking, whatever you want to call it. They're just people on the environmental modeling contract, but they're very organized. I'm here because I'm pretty sure they've been tracking my revisions and planting those errors in the datasets to make it look like I can't lead the work. Even when my wife or the junior analysts tell me it's just version-control mistakes, I know what's really happening. It's just regular people using computers to mess with me. 

Computers... they've really changed everything, haven't they? I remember when we first got a computer at home, back in the early nineties. It was a big clunky thing, a desktop, took up half the desk. The monitor was as deep as a microwave oven. We had dial-up internet, and it made that awful screeching noise when it connected. My daughter used to get so mad if someone picked up the phone while she was trying to talk to her friends on AIM. AIM... AOL Instant Messenger. Kids don't use that anymore. Now everyone just texts. My grandson texts me sometimes, but he uses all these abbreviations I don't understand. SMH, TBH, IDK. It's like a whole different language. 

I tried to learn Spanish once, back in college. I only took a couple of semesters, though. I thought it would be useful, but I never really had a knack for languages. Math, that was my thing. Numbers make sense. They follow rules. Languages have too many exceptions to the rules. Like the word "read" and "read." Spelled the same, pronounced differently. How does anyone learn English? It must be a nightmare. I had a roommate in college who was an English major. He read all these massive books. Tolstoy, Dostoevsky. He tried to get me to read Crime and Punishment, but I couldn't get past the first chapter. Too depressing. I prefer non-fiction. History, mostly. The Civil War era is fascinating. The strategies they used... 

But anyway, no, no special powers. Just the contract people messing with my files.

Even though there is no objective proof and others have given alternative explanations for the errors in the datasets, do you still believe, without any doubt, that your coworkers are intentionally sabotaging your work as part of a coordinated effort?

Oh, absolutely. Coordinated effort is exactly what it is. I mean, I've said it before, I'm here because I'm pretty sure the people on that environmental modeling contract have been tracking my revisions and planting errors in the datasets just to make it look like I can't lead the work. My wife and the junior analysts keep telling me it's just version-control mistakes, but I know what I'm seeing. 

Those junior analysts, they're so young, you know? Barely out of their twenties. They think they know everything because they can write a few Python scripts. When I got my first real job, I was doing land surveying. We had to carry these incredibly heavy tripods and theodolites all over the county. Summer of '84, I think it was. It was so hot that year, the asphalt on the roads was literally melting. You'd step on it and your shoe would just sink right in. I ruined a perfectly good pair of work boots that way. Good leather ones, too. I bought them at Sears. 

You remember Sears, right? They used to have everything. Tools, clothes, appliances. My grandfather actually bought his whole house from a Sears catalog back in the 1920s. It came on a train, all the pieces numbered, and he put it together himself with his brother. Can you imagine that? Buying a whole house out of a catalog? Now everything is just cheap particle board and plastic. Nobody builds things to last anymore. It's all disposable, you use it for a year and throw it in the landfill. It's terrible for the environment, really. 

But anyway... yes, to answer your question, there is no doubt in my mind about the sabotage. I know they're doing it.

Computers... they've really changed everything, haven't they? I remember when we first got a computer at home, back in the early nineties. It was a big clunky thing, a desktop, took up half the desk. The monitor was as deep as a microwave oven. We had dial-up internet, and it made that awful screeching noise when it connected.
